extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York and the United States debating the proposed Constitution; engaged readers of The Federalist Papers
extracted.subtask_description: A political-legal essay analyzing and defending the powers conferred by the proposed U.S. Constitution, explaining why particular federal powers are necessary and how abuses should be guarded against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity Principle for Government Powers
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether to confer a power, the first question is whether such a power is necessary to attain a necessary public end; choices must aim for the greater (not perfect) good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not focus solely on possible inconveniences or abuses; evaluate whether the power is an appropriate means to an essential public objective. The essay emphasizes choosing a power that advances public happiness even if it brings unavoidable alloy, and assessing necessity before judging potential abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against Perversion of Necessary Powers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a power is judged necessary, the next duty is to guard as effectually as possible against its perversion to public detriment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When granting authority, include structural or temporal constraints (e.g., appropriations limits) and other safeguards. The text repeatedly argues for combining necessary powers with prudential checks to minimize abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union as a Safeguard Against Dangerous Standing Armies
rubrics_metrics.description: A united nation reduces the need for large standing armies and therefore helps protect liberty — disunion would make standing armies more likely and more dangerous to liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument: a united America presents a more formidable posture to foreign ambition with fewer troops; disunion would force each state/confederacy to maintain larger forces, leading to perpetual taxes and threats to liberties. This is presented as a policy criterion favoring a stronger federal union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit Appropriations for Military Support (Term Limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the term for which revenue may be appropriated to support standing armies (the Constitution's two-year appropriation term is a prudent guard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison with British practice: though British practice limits army appropriations practically to one year, the Constitution's two-year maximum is justified given freeness of American elections; such temporal limits are a safeguard against long-term military establishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Discretion to Raise and Maintain Forces (Including Peacetime Readiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers to raise armies and provide fleets (and maintain readiness in peace as well as war) are involved in self-defense and must not be rigidly limited by constitutional barriers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues it would be imprudent to limit defensive preparedness when offensive threats cannot be similarly limited; prohibiting peacetime preparedness invites vulnerabilities and precedents for usurpation when ad hoc needs arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated Powers Must Qualify the General Welfare Phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: The general phrase granting power 'to lay and collect taxes... to provide for the common defense and general welfare' must be read in light of the subsequent specific enumerations — the particulars explain and qualify the general expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects the interpretation that the general welfare clause alone grants unlimited legislative authority. The existence of an immediately following specification of powers demonstrates the intent to limit the scope of the general phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Authority over Treaties and Diplomatic Representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Power to make treaties and to send and receive ambassadors, other public ministers, and consuls properly belongs to the federal government and must be coherent and sufficiently broad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties and diplomatic appointments should not be frustrated by conflicting state regulations; the Constitution improves on the Confederation by explicitly including lower grades of ministers and consular functions to ensure practical foreign relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to Define and Punish Piracies and High-seas Felonies (Uniformity Required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government must have the power to define and punish piracies and felonies on the high seas and offenses against the law of nations, to ensure certainty and uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on varied state codes or the common law of another country would produce inconsistency; legislative definition at the federal level ensures uniform rules across the Union and prevents individual states embroiling the Confederacy with foreign nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Regulation of Foreign Commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulating intercourse with foreign nations, including foreign commerce, is an essential federal power; it must be centralized to provide effective national policy (including the postponed power to prohibit importation of slaves until 1808).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign commerce regulation must be coherent and effective; the twenty-year postponement on prohibiting slave importation is presented as a politically necessary concession that still represents a moral and humanitarian gain over the status quo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Regulation of Interstate Commerce to Prevent Parochial Harms
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to regulate commerce among the several States is necessary to prevent states from imposing tolls, duties, or other burdens on goods passing through their jurisdiction that would create animosities and interrupt tranquility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience shows that without a superintending authority, states will enact measures (tolls, duties) that unfairly burden other states' commerce, provoking retaliation and instability; examples from Switzerland and the German empire illustrate these problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for Uniform National Standards (Money, Weights, Naturalization, Bankruptcy, Postal System)
rubrics_metrics.description: Powers such as coining money and regulating its value, fixing standards of weights and measures, establishing uniform naturalization and bankruptcy laws, and creating post offices/roads must be federal to secure certainty and uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divergent state practices would impede commerce, justice, and governance; uniform rules at the federal level are presented as essential to the Union's practical functioning and longevity.
